issues: Quote is verbatim on the live NDSS PDF, and the value 3,603, the unit, 'late May' and the 6,579-site / 28-country / top-500 frame all match (abstract: 'For each country, we periodically examined its 500 most popular websites - 6,579 in total'). Crossref (DOI 10.14722/ndss.2019.23378) confirms NDSS 2019, San Diego, Internet Society, and the six authors.

The notes say the growth happened 'most of it around the GDPR'. That is wrong if it means the deadline. Of the 1,458 words added (2,145 to 3,603, +68%, so 'about two-thirds' is right), 899 (62%) were added between March 2016 and March 2018. Only 559 (38%) came in the roughly two months before 25 May 2018. The paper's 'another 18 percentage points' is measured against the March 2018 length (3,603/3,044 = +18%), not the 2016 base (which would be +26 points).

The notes leave out a population caveat. The March 2016 (and 2017) lengths come from Internet Archive copies. The paper says 'On average, we were able to access previous versions for 2,187 policies for each month'. So the 2016 mean is not over all 6,579 sites, and the three means are not necessarily over the same set of policies. The authors also did not compare lengths across countries because of language differences (footnote 9).

The notes' parenthetical about Amos et al. is confirmed. Amos et al. (arXiv 2008.09159v4) write 'Degaling et al. found the median privacy policy word count ... to be 2,145 in 2016 ... and 3,044 in 2018', while Degeling et al. say 'mean'. Added as an independent source.

The rest, an 18% rise on the March 2018 length, came in the two months before the GDPR took effect on 25 May 2018. The 2016 figure is based on Internet Archive copies (on average 2,187 policies a month could be retrieved), so the three means are not necessarily over the same set of sites. The authors did not compare lengths across countries because of language differences. (Amos et al. 2021 cite the 2016 and 2018 figures as medians; Degeling et al. describe them as means.)

issues: Both quotes are verbatim in the live ICCL PDF. 747, Colorado 987, District of Columbia 486 ('D.C. day time commuter adjusted population used') and the lowest state, Mississippi 493, all match the per-person chart on p. 3.

The 747 is not total U.S. broadcasts divided by population. It equals the simple unweighted mean of ICCL's 51 state and D.C. figures (746.7). ICCL's own total of 294 billion a day divided by the 2021 U.S. population (about 332 million) gives about 886, or about 984 if divided by 90% of the population. The notes should say what the 747 is.

The notes misdescribe the stated method. They say per-person figures 'divide by population assuming 90% of people are online'. The published state and country figures instead match 0.9 x daily broadcasts / total population, within 1%, for every state or country where the report gives a daily total: California 35bn gives 803 (published 804), Texas 24.5bn gives 747 (748), Florida 21bn gives 868 (870), Germany 30.8bn gives 333 (334), France 25.4bn gives 339 (340), using 2021 census and Eurostat populations. Dividing by 90% of the population would give figures about 23% higher. The UK (31.9bn a day, published 462) fits neither method.
'State averages range from 987 (Colorado) to 486 (District of Columbia...)': D.C. is not a state. Reworded to 'state and D.C. figures'.

The report does not reconcile internally. ICCL says 'People in the U.S. have their online activity and real-world location exposed 57% more often than people in Europe', but 747 vs 376 is 99% more. The Europe 376 also seems to use a different method (see the Europe verdict), so the U.S. and Europe headline averages should not be compared directly.
The notes leave out ICCL's own caveat. The report calls its figures 'a low estimate' because the industry data exclude Facebook and Amazon RTB broadcasts.

No independent source reproduces the figure, because the underlying industry data are confidential. The session's web-search budget was exhausted, so press coverage could not be looked for. The record is kept as a clearly labelled advocacy estimate. Year 2022 (publication 16 May 2022, per the page's article:published_time) is right.

fieldFixes.notes: ICCL's 747 is the simple (unweighted) average of its 51 state and D.C. figures. These range from 987 (Colorado) to 486 (District of Columbia, commuter-adjusted population). ICCL's own U.S. total of 294 billion broadcasts a day divided by the U.S. population would give about 886. ICCL says the industry counts of RTB broadcasts over 30 days come from a confidential source, and that it assumes 90% of each population is online. The published figures do not follow that method exactly. State and country figures match 0.9 x daily broadcasts / total population (California 35bn a day gives 804, Germany 30.8bn gives 334), not broadcasts / (0.9 x population). ICCL calls its figures a low estimate because the industry data exclude Facebook and Amazon RTB broadcasts. Advocacy estimate, not independently audited: treat as an order-of-magnitude figure, and do not compare it directly with the Europe average of 376, which appears to be computed differently.

issues: All three quotes are verbatim in the live Princeton PDF (extended version of the CCS 2016 paper). 81,000, 123 sites above 1%, 'over 90 million requests' and January 2016 all match. Crossref (DOI 10.1145/2976749.2978313) confirms CCS'16, Vienna, Austria, published 24 Oct 2016, pp. 1388-1401, authors Englehardt and Narayanan.

The notes repeat 'Google, Facebook, Twitter and AdNexus were the only third-party entities on more than 10% of sites' without the qualification in the same section. Grouping domains by parent organization, the paper says 'Google, Facebook, Twitter, Amazon, AdNexus, and Oracle are the third-party organizations present on more than 10% of sites' (Figure 3). Readers will take 'entities' to mean companies, so both counts should be given.

Missing caveats that change how the number should be read. (a) A 'third party' is any domain (public suffix + 1) other than the landing page's, not necessarily a tracker: 'Every third party is potentially a tracker, but for many of our results we need a more conservative definition'. Content-delivery domains such as gstatic.com and fbcdn.net are counted. (b) The crawler visited only each site's homepage: 'The browser does not interact with the site or visit any other pages within the site'. (c) Statistics cover the 917,261 sites that loaded successfully, not a full million.

No independent secondary source repeating 81,000 could be found (webtap.princeton.edu returned 502, the ACM DL 403, and the web-search budget was exhausted). The Freedom to Tinker release post (18 May 2016) confirms the study but gives no figures.

fieldFixes.notes: A long tail: only 123 of these 81,000 were present on more than 1% of sites. A 'third party' here is any outside domain loaded by a site's homepage, not necessarily a tracker (content-delivery domains count too). The crawl visited only homepages of the 917,261 sites that loaded, making over 90 million requests. All top 5 third parties and 12 of the top 20 were Google-owned domains. Google, Facebook, Twitter and AdNexus were the only third-party entities on more than 10% of sites. Grouped by parent organization, the paper counts six: Google, Facebook, Twitter, Amazon, AdNexus and Oracle.

issues: Both quotes are verbatim in the live FTC PDF (dated May 2014; released 27 May 2014). The nine brokers, the section 6(b) orders ('in December 2012, the Commission initiated a study'), the 'starting January 1, 2010' scope and the broker-to-broker sourcing claim all match. 'None of the nine data brokers collect data directly from consumers' supports the notes' paraphrase.
